To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the concentrations of oxalate and other organic acids in stratocumuli cloudwater samples collected in the northeastern Pacific are strongly influenced by the wind speed, that a sharp reduction in oxalate concentration is observed in three case flights, and that the reduction in oxalates is likely due to photolysis of oxalato complexes.

(1) oxalate concentrations in cloudwater are strongly correlated to wind speed, suggesting that an important oxalate source is via gaseous emissions from the ocean surface; (2) oxalate and Fe concentrations were inversely correlated in cloudwater, suggesting that the photochemical destruction of Fe oxalato complexes may be an important oxalato sink; and (3) oxalate was the only organic acid whose concentrations decreased by an order of magnitude in three case flights,

(1) oxalate and other organic acid concentrations are positively correlated with low level wind speed suggesting an important source of oxalate is from the ocean; (2) oxalate concentrations drop by nearly one order of magnitude relative in the same region of cloud, and (3) the photolysis rate of iron oxalate complexes is an important sink for oxalate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the chemical evolution of organic acid species in marine cloudwater.
the sources and sinks of organic acids and metals in marine clouds.
the sources of organic acids and the role of iron oxalate complexes in the oxidation of organic acids in the marine boundary layer of the northeastern Pacific Ocean.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the observed oxalate reductions are likely due to a combination of metal complexation and photolysis.
the production and loss of oxalates in cloud water is a complex process involving many factors.
the photochemical oxidation of organic compounds in clouds is the dominant pathway for oxalate production in the northeastern Pacific Ocean region.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ocean is a major source of oxalate and that its removal in clouds is dominated by photolytic loss from iron oxalato complexation.
oxalate is produced in the marine boundary layer by a variety of processes, but it is rapidly removed by photolysis of metal oxalato complexes.
oxalate is a ubiquitous organic acid in the northeastern Pacific stratocumulus layer, with concentrations ranging from 1.5 to 6.6 μM.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a significant fraction of the organic acid concentrations in stratocumuluss clouds is due to metal-organic interactions and that this fraction is likely to be a significant source of uncertainty for the organic aerosol budget in the marine boundary layer.
the presence of metals, especially Fe, in clouds is an important factor in determining the extent to which organic acids are reduced in clouds.
oxalate production is a complex process involving multiple sources and sinks and that the role of metals in oxalate chemistry should be considered when modeling the atmospheric chemistry of oxalate.
